blocks.text: The third shape handles problems asking about **three or more** elements. The idea is to reduce the harder problem to one you have already solved.

Finding three numbers that sum to a target looks like a triple nested loop — O(N³). But fix one of the three, and what remains is: *find two numbers summing to `target - fixed`*. That is exactly the reduction shape.

items: **Fix** the first element by looping over every index `i`.
**Run two pointers** on everything to the right of `i`, looking for `target - arr[i]`.

blocks.text: One outer loop of N iterations, each running an O(N) two pointer scan: **O(N²)**. Plus O(N log N) to sort, which is dominated.
Down from O(N³). The same trick extends — four numbers becomes two nested fixes plus a scan, giving O(N³) instead of O(N⁴).
**Start `left` at `i + 1`, never at 0.** The elements before `i` were already fully explored as the fixed element, and reusing them produces duplicate triples in a different order.
**Skip duplicates** when the problem wants unique results. After a match, advance past any repeated values:

blocks.code:
while (left < right && arr[left] === arr[left + 1]) left++;
while (left < right && arr[right] === arr[right - 1]) right--;

blocks.text: Sorting is what makes this cheap — equal values sit together, so skipping them is a local check rather than a search.
When a problem asks for k elements meeting a condition and k > 2, try fixing k − 2 of them and running two pointers on the rest. It is the standard move.
